title: Relocating and Need to Sell Your House Fast? Here's Exactly What to Do
excerpt: When a job transfer, family situation, or fresh start forces you to move quickly, selling your home on your timeline — not the market's — becomes the top priority. This guide walks you through every option, with real numbers and actionable steps to close fast without leaving money on the table.

sections.content: A job offer lands in your inbox on a Tuesday. The start date is six weeks away — in another city, maybe another state. Suddenly, selling your home goes from a someday project to an urgent priority. If you're relocating and need to sell your house fast, you're not alone. The National Association of Realtors estimates that job relocation drives roughly 17% of all home sales in the U.S. each year. The good news? You have more options than you might think — and some of them can put cash in your hand in as little as 7 to 14 days.
Why Relocation Sales Are Different (And More Urgent)

A typical home sale in the U.S. takes 30 to 60 days just to get an accepted offer, and another 30 to 45 days to close. That's potentially 90 days of carrying costs — mortgage payments, utilities, insurance, and property taxes — on a home you're no longer living in. If you're already paying rent in your new city, those dual costs add up fast. At an average mortgage payment of $2,000 per month, every extra month you wait could cost you $2,000 to $3,000 or more after factoring in all holding costs.
The biggest mistake relocating sellers make is waiting too long to list. Every month you delay is a month you're paying two housing bills. Speed and pricing strategy matter more than perfection.
Your Three Main Options When You Need to Sell Fast
Option 1: Sell to a Cash Buyer or Investor

This is the fastest route available. Cash buyers — including real estate investors and wholesalers — can close in as few as 7 to 21 days with no financing contingencies, no appraisal delays, and minimal back-and-forth. You typically skip repairs, showings, and open houses entirely. The trade-off is price: cash offers usually come in at 70% to 85% of the home's after-repair value (ARV). On a home worth $300,000 in market-ready condition, that might mean an offer between $210,000 and $255,000. For many relocating sellers, the certainty and speed are worth more than squeezing out every last dollar — especially when you're racing against a job start date.

Before accepting any cash offer, run the numbers yourself. Use the free [Deal Calculator at aiwholesail.com/tools/wholesale-deal-calculator](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/wholesale-deal-calculator) to estimate your home's true value and make sure the offer you receive is fair based on real market data.
Option 2: Price Aggressively and List on the MLS

If you have a few extra weeks and want to maximize your sale price, pricing your home 5% to 10% below comparable sales in your neighborhood is a proven way to generate fast, competitive interest. Homes priced competitively often receive multiple offers within the first 7 to 10 days. Hire an experienced local agent who understands your timeline, request a pre-listing inspection so there are no surprises, and make the home available for showings immediately. This approach can net you significantly more than a cash buyer offer, especially in hot markets like [Atlanta](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/atlanta-ga), [Dallas](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx), or [Phoenix](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/phoenix-az), where buyer demand remains strong.
Option 3: iBuyer Programs

Companies like Opendoor and Offerpad use automated valuation tools to make instant offers on qualifying homes. Timelines are typically 14 to 30 days, and prices land somewhere between a traditional cash offer and a full market sale — usually 90% to 95% of market value, minus a service fee of 5% to 8%. iBuyers work best on homes that are in good condition, built after 1960, and located in suburban markets they actively serve. If your home needs significant repairs or sits in a rural area, iBuyer programs may pass on your property entirely.
A Step-by-Step Plan to Sell Your Home Before You Move

items: Step 1 — Know your deadline. Pin down your exact move date and work backward. If you need to be out in 45 days, you need an offer accepted within the next 7 to 10 days to close on time with traditional financing, or within 30 days if selling to a cash buyer.

Step 2 — Get a realistic price estimate. Pull recent comparable sales (comps) within a half mile and the last 90 days. Adjust for square footage, condition, and upgrades. An agent's CMA or an online ARV tool can help you land on a number that moves fast.

Step 3 — Decide which sale method fits your situation. If speed is everything, go cash buyer first. If you have a little more runway, try aggressive MLS pricing for 7 to 10 days before pivoting to investor offers.

Step 4 — Declutter and clean immediately. You don't need to renovate. A deep clean, fresh paint in neutral tones, and strong listing photos can meaningfully boost buyer interest without costing more than $500 to $1,500.

Step 5 — Request a leaseback option if needed. Some buyers — especially investors — will allow you to lease the property back for 30 to 60 days after closing. This lets you collect your sale proceeds before your move is fully complete.
Step 6 — Disclose everything upfront. Nothing kills a fast close faster than surprise inspection findings. Proactively disclosing known issues keeps your deal on track and builds buyer trust.
Step 7 — Line up your moving logistics in parallel. Contact movers, arrange storage if needed, and notify your lender about the payoff timeline so there are no last-minute delays at closing.

sections.content: What Investors Look for in Relocation Properties

Understanding how investors think can help you negotiate better terms. Real estate investors are looking for motivated sellers — and relocation is one of the clearest signs of motivation. They calculate offers based on the ARV minus repair costs minus their target profit margin, typically following the 70% rule. If your home needs $20,000 in repairs and has an ARV of $280,000, a standard investor formula produces a maximum offer of around $176,000. Knowing this math before you sit across the table puts you in a stronger negotiating position. For a deeper look at how investors evaluate deals, check out this guide on [how to find off-market real estate deals](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/off-market-real-estate-deals).

If your home is in solid condition, mention it upfront when reaching out to investors. A move-in-ready property with no deferred maintenance can command 80% to 90% of ARV even in a cash sale, rather than the standard 70% to 75%.
How Real Estate Wholesalers Can Help You Sell Fast

Wholesalers are a specific type of real estate investor who specialize in connecting motivated sellers with cash buyers quickly. Rather than buying your home themselves, a wholesaler puts your property under contract and assigns that contract to an end buyer — often closing in 10 to 21 days. For relocating sellers, this can be an efficient path to a fast close. If you're new to how this works or want to understand what's happening on the buyer's side of the table, the [Wholesaling Real Estate for Beginners guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/wholesaling-real-estate-for-beginners) breaks the entire process down in plain language.
Common Mistakes to Avoid When Selling Due to Relocation

items: Overpricing because of emotional attachment — the market doesn't care what you paid or what you owe.
Waiting to list until after you've moved — vacant homes sit longer and feel less appealing to buyers.
Accepting the first offer without getting at least 2 to 3 competing quotes, even from cash buyers.
Forgetting to account for closing costs, agent commissions (if applicable), and mortgage payoff when calculating your net proceeds.
Skipping the leaseback conversation — many sellers leave this option on the table entirely.

sections.content: In real estate, carrying costs are silent killers. A home that sits unsold for 90 extra days often ends up netting the same — or less — than a well-priced fast sale would have produced on day one.

Relocating is stressful enough without your home sale adding to the chaos. Whether you choose to sell to a cash buyer, list aggressively on the MLS, or explore an iBuyer program, the key is making a clear-eyed decision early — before your timeline forces your hand. Run your numbers, understand your options, and move decisively. The sellers who do best in relocation scenarios are the ones who treat the home sale as a logistics problem to solve, not a financial opportunity to maximize at all costs.
